post.description:
Throttled to 5 attempts a minute per client address.

Unthrottled, an 8-character password over this endpoint is a matter of
patience. user_repo.authenticate also runs bcrypt unconditionally, so an
unknown email costs the same as a known one — the response time no longer
reveals which accounts exist.

get.description:
The accounts a developer may become. Development only; 404 when off.

This exists so the client does not have to keep its own copy of the
allow-list — the server owns it, and the UI renders whatever it is told.

It also solves a problem the POST cannot: that endpoint answers 404 both
when the flag is off AND when the address is not allow-listed, on purpose,
so a caller cannot enumerate the personas from it. Which means the POST is
useless for asking "is this feature available?". This is that question,
asked once.

Listing the fixtures when the flag is on is not a leak: they are seeded
test accounts, and anything that can read this can already mint tokens for
them.

schema.title: Response List Demo Personas Api V1 Auth Demo Persona Get

post.description:
Sign in as a seeded demo account WITHOUT a password. Development only.

This is impersonation, so it is fenced in four ways:

1. `settings.ENABLE_DEMO_PERSONAS` defaults to False, and this returns
   **404** when it is off rather than 401 or 403, with byte-identical
   body to FastAPI's own 404 — so probing for the route learns nothing.

   Two holes in that claim were found in review and closed here. The
   detail string was "Not found" against FastAPI's "Not Found", which
   distinguished a disabled route from an absent one on capitalisation
   alone. And `include_in_schema` was left at its default, so
   `/api/v1/openapi.json` — which this app serves unconditionally, in
   every environment — published the route, its request model and its
   response model regardless of the flag. Masking the response while
   publishing the schema is not masking.

   NOTE: `include_in_schema` is evaluated at import time, so flipping the
   flag needs a restart to change what the schema shows. That is correct
   for a deploy-time flag and would be wrong for a runtime one.
2. The target must appear in `settings.DEMO_PERSONA_EMAILS`, an explicit
   allow-list of seeded fixtures. Even with the flag wrongly enabled, this
   cannot mint a token for a real person's account.
3. The account must still exist and be active, so a disabled fixture stays
   disabled.
4. Rate-limited on the same budget as /login, so it is no cheaper to abuse.

It issues a genuine token pair through `session_service.issue`, exactly as
/login does. That is deliberate: a parallel token path would be a second
thing to get wrong, and the resulting session must be revocable and
refreshable like any other.

Exchange a refresh token for a new pair.

The access token now lives 30 minutes instead of 8 days, which is only
tolerable because this endpoint exists — shortening the lifetime without a
refresh path logs everyone out mid-task.

Refresh tokens ROTATE: the presented one is invalidated and a new one
issued. Re-presenting a rotated token means either a race or a theft, and
the service revokes the whole family rather than guessing which.

End this session.

Deliberately takes the refresh token rather than the access token: the
access token expires on its own shortly, and it is the refresh token that
would otherwise keep the session alive for a fortnight.

Not authenticated — a user whose access token has already expired must
still be able to sign out, and presenting a valid refresh token is proof
enough to end that one session.

End every session for the current user.

The thing a JWT alone can never do, and the reason refresh tokens are
stored server-side.

get.description:
Every club this user can open a workspace for, and in what capacity.

Three sources, unioned:
  1. active student memberships,
  2. faculty coordinator assignments — faculty_scope.get_club_coordinator_club_ids()
     has existed since Phase 7 with ZERO call sites repo-wide, which is
     precisely why a Faculty Coordinator's selector came back empty and he
     could never reach the club whose plan he was supposed to approve,
  3. department-wide reviewers (Cultural Coordinator, HOD), who oversee
     every club.

Filtered in SQL rather than by post-filtering club_repo.get_multi(): that
call was LIMIT 100 with no ORDER BY, so a user whose only membership was
club #101 got an empty selector and no error at all.

Record who attended an event.

correcting one student's attendance — or simply saving the register twice —

get.description:
The class's timetable, narrowed to the caller's batch by default.

A student is only ever shown slots they actually sit in: their own batch's,
plus every unbatched slot. Left unfiltered, the claim wizard offered the
other batch's hours, and a claim raised against one routed to a faculty
member who does not teach that student — which no reviewer could sensibly
approve or refuse.

Anyone who is not a student (Class Teacher, HOD, admin) gets the whole grid
unless they ask for a batch explicitly, since maintaining a timetable means
seeing all of it.

get.description:
Claims scoped to what this caller may see, one page at a time.

Returns an envelope with a TOTAL rather than a bare array. The previous
100-row cap was invisible: a super_admin with 300 claims saw 100 and no
indication the rest existed. An explicit page with a total is the opposite
failure mode — the user can see there is more.

Scoping happens first and pagination second, on purpose: paging a list and
then filtering it would produce short pages and a meaningless total.

`view` splits a reviewer's claims into what still needs them and what they
have already decided. It does nothing for a student: their own claims are
their own claims whatever state they are in.

The claim state machine, as data.

ClaimStatusStepper.tsx kept its own hardcoded copy of the stage list and
labels — which is how it came to hardcode 'approved' onto stage 3 as a
workaround for a backend bug, permanently greying out the stage that
actually needed attention. Serving the same table both sides read from
removes the temptation.

MUST stay above the /{claim_id} route below, or "workflow" is matched as
a claim id and this endpoint never runs — the same trap that hid the
reviewer inbox in clubs.py.

post.description:
Advance, return or reject a claim at whichever stage it is sitting in.

This was a 130-line if/elif chain, and three separate defects in it were
really one defect: a branch that forgot to honour `action` (a rejection
recorded as a success), a branch that forgot super_admin (an admin unable
to rescue a stuck claim), and a branch that forgot to record the revision.
Each was patched individually.

The stages now live in app/core/claim_workflow.STAGES, and this endpoint is
the three steps that are true of every stage: look up the spec, authorize,
apply. A new stage cannot forget any of them.

get.description:
Everything waiting on this user, from every module, most urgent first.

Nobody logs in wanting "the Clubs module" — they log in because something
needs them. Every input for this already existed in the database and
nothing aggregated it, which is the deeper reason the Faculty Coordinator
never approved his club's annual plan: not that he could not navigate to
it, but that nothing ever told him it was there.

put.description:
Let people turn email off.

A system that emails you about things you did not ask to hear about, with
no way to stop it, gets filtered wholesale — including the messages that
actually needed you.

post.description:
Run the digest.

An endpoint rather than an in-process timer: a timer inside a web worker
fires once PER WORKER, so a three-worker deployment sends three copies of
every digest. Point a scheduler at this instead.

get.description:
Where every item in both workflows is stuck, and for how long.

The claim state machine and the annual-plan state machine both worked and
neither was visible in aggregate: you could ask how ONE claim was doing,
and nothing could tell you that six had been sitting at subject-faculty
review for a fortnight.

SLA days are per STAGE, because that is where work stalls — and the stage
that stalls is the one with many possible reviewers and therefore nobody
who feels responsible.

What is waiting on the caller's decision right now, oldest first.

Scoped in SQL, the same way the review endpoints authorize, so the count is
honest: a Faculty Coordinator sees only their own clubs' forms, and a form
whose event has started is gone — nobody can act on it any more.

Everything the caller has approved, sent back or rejected, newest first.

Only what they may still read: a reviewer who has lost the role, or a
Faculty Coordinator moved off the club, keeps no window onto the forms.
Forms and claim sheets the caller is listed on, once the club has submitted them.

ClubBootstrap.title: ClubBootstrap
ClubBootstrap.description:
One request per workspace mount.

Mounting the Clubs workspace used to issue THIRTEEN requests. Of those
payloads exactly three are needed by more than one tab, so the right shape
is a small composed shell plus a lazy fetch per tab — not one mega-endpoint
that re-sends everything.

visible_tabs is the important field: the server decides what a coordinator
versus a member may see, which is what stops the UI offering actions the
backend will 403.

Everything the viewer is allowed to DO in this club, resolved server-side.

Generalizes the three viewer_can_* flags on ClubDetailOut into the full
set. The frontend must never re-derive scope logic — that is how the UI
ends up rendering six buttons the backend will refuse.

One student's attendance at one event.

directly, so a malformed record was a 500 rather than a 422 naming the

A real model, not List[dict].

task.py indexed item["title"] and item["assignee_id"] directly, so an
action item missing either was a 500 rather than a 422 telling the user
which field they left out.

MyClubOut.title: MyClubOut
MyClubOut.description:
A club in the user's own selector, plus WHY it is there.

The relationship drives the UI: a faculty_coordinator is not a member and
must not be shown member-only tabs or write actions, and a department-wide
reviewer is looking at a club they oversee rather than one they belong to.
Without this the selector could only say "here are some clubs".

The stepper could say WHICH DESK a claim sat on but never WHO, and at the
subject-faculty stage that is the only useful question — the claim waits
on every subject faculty member independently, so "under review" could
mean one signature outstanding or four.

Distinct from ProgrammeOut, which is the admin/storage shape: outcomes and
careers are comma-joined strings in the database and real lists on the
wire. Without a response_model the generated OpenAPI schema described the
storage shape, and the frontend was typed against strings it then called

UserProfileOut.description:
Response shape for GET /auth/me only. Carries the resolved permission
set and the platform capability map in the SAME payload the frontend
already fetches at session hydrate, so the frontend never needs (and
must never re-introduce) its own copy of either registry.
